questions.question: SQL vs NoSQL vs NewSQL — how do you choose a database for a new system?
questions.title: SQL vs NoSQL vs NewSQL: Choosing a Database
questions.direct_answer: Start with **relational (Postgres/MySQL)** unless you have a concrete reason not to — ACID, joins, mature tooling, familiar query model. Go **NoSQL** when the access pattern is truly key-value (DynamoDB, Redis), document-shaped with flexible schema (MongoDB), wide-column at massive scale (Cassandra, ScyllaDB), or graph (Neo4j). Go **NewSQL** (CockroachDB, Spanner, YugabyteDB) when you need both horizontal scale and strong SQL semantics — global consistency, distributed transactions. The wrong question is 'SQL or NoSQL?' — the right one is 'what are my read/write patterns, consistency needs, and scale requirements?' Most systems ship with Postgres and evolve; polyglot persistence emerges as needed.

interviewer_intent.testing: Pragmatic database selection; understanding CAP and real workload patterns
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Defaulting to NoSQL for 'scale' without needing it; thinking Postgres doesn't scale; picking MongoDB for relational data
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss CAP vs PACELC, workload patterns (OLTP, OLAP, HTAP), access patterns driving schema (DynamoDB single-table), write amplification, global distribution, cost

sections.title: The Database Landscape in 2026
sections.content:
There are more database categories than there used to be. A useful mental map:

**Relational (SQL)** — Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle. Decades of maturity. ACID transactions. Normalized schemas with joins. Rich query language. Great for OLTP, most business applications, anything with relationships. Postgres has become remarkable in 2026 — JSONB, full-text search, geospatial (PostGIS), pub/sub (LISTEN/NOTIFY), logical replication, TimescaleDB extension for time-series. Reaches petabyte scale with Citus/CockroachDB-like extensions.

**Key-Value NoSQL** — Redis, DynamoDB, Memcached. O(1) lookup by key; no relations. Ultra-fast. Redis is in-memory with persistence options; great for caching, sessions, rate limiters, leaderboards. DynamoDB is AWS-managed, scales automatically, great for key-based access patterns; needs careful schema design (single-table or access-pattern-driven).

**Document NoSQL** — MongoDB, Couchbase, Elastic (as document store). Schema-flexible JSON-like documents. No rigid schema; good for rapidly evolving data shapes. Weaker for joins and transactions (MongoDB has multi-document transactions now but use sparingly).

**Wide-Column NoSQL** — Cassandra, ScyllaDB, HBase, BigTable. Tables with flexible columns per row. Optimized for writes and linear scaling. Eventual consistency by default. Great for time-series, IoT, event logs at massive scale. Designed for the access pattern first; change access pattern later = redesign.

**Graph** — Neo4j, Amazon Neptune, TigerGraph. Nodes and edges. Best when traversals dominate (social networks, fraud rings, knowledge graphs).

**NewSQL / Distributed SQL** — CockroachDB, Google Spanner, YugabyteDB, TiDB. SQL + ACID + horizontal scaling. The 'have your cake and eat it too' category. Pay latency (cross-region consensus) for consistency.

**OLAP / Data Warehouse** — Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, ClickHouse, DuckDB. Columnar, optimized for analytics; not for OLTP. Separate from your transactional DB.

**Search** — Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Typesense, Meilisearch. Full-text search, faceting. Used alongside primary DB.

**Time-Series** — InfluxDB, TimescaleDB (Postgres extension), Prometheus. Optimized for time-stamped metrics.

**Vector** — Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, pgvector. For embeddings / RAG / AI retrieval.

Most systems use multiple: Postgres primary + Redis cache + Elasticsearch search + S3 blobs + Snowflake analytics. This is **polyglot persistence**.

sections.title: When Each Shines
sections.content:
| Category | Examples | Strengths | Weaknesses | Typical Use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Relational** | Postgres, MySQL | ACID, joins, mature, flexible queries | Vertical scaling first; sharding is work | OLTP, most web apps |
| **Key-Value** | Redis, DynamoDB | O(1) lookup, horizontal scale | No joins, access-pattern-driven schema | Cache, sessions, rate limit, KV by id |
| **Document** | MongoDB, Couchbase | Flexible schema, nested | Joins weak, transactions limited | Rapid evolving shapes, CMS |
| **Wide-Column** | Cassandra, Scylla | Massive write throughput, linear scale | Eventual consistency, schema-rigid for queries | Time-series, IoT, events |
| **Graph** | Neo4j, Neptune | Traversal queries, cyclic relationships | Harder to scale, niche | Social, fraud, recommendations |
| **NewSQL** | Cockroach, Spanner | SQL + horizontal + ACID | Cross-region latency, cost, complexity | Global SaaS needing consistency |
| **OLAP** | Snowflake, BigQuery, ClickHouse | Columnar, fast aggregates over big data | Not for OLTP, slow single-row | Analytics, reporting, BI |
| **Search** | Elasticsearch, OpenSearch | Full-text, faceting, ranking | Not a source of truth, cost | Site search, log aggregation |
| **Time-Series** | InfluxDB, TimescaleDB | Optimized for time-range | Less flexible schema | Metrics, telemetry |
| **Vector** | Pinecone, Weaviate, pgvector | Similarity search on embeddings | New category, tooling maturing | RAG, semantic search |

sections.title: Decision Framework
sections.content:
**Step 1: Understand your workload**

- **OLTP** (online transaction processing): short reads/writes, high concurrency, consistency matters (e-commerce, banking, SaaS)
- **OLAP** (analytical): long scans, aggregates, low concurrency, eventual freshness OK (reporting, BI)
- **HTAP** (hybrid): both — often solved by separate OLTP DB + pipeline to OLAP
- **Real-time / streaming**: append-heavy, time-based queries (metrics, logs)
- **Search**: full-text, ranking, faceting

**Step 2: Understand your access patterns**

- How do you read? By primary key, by range, by join, by text, by similarity?
- How do you write? Append-only, updates in place, bulk inserts?
- What's the read:write ratio?
- What's the scale in rows, operations per second, data size?
- What's the consistency requirement? Strong, read-your-writes, eventual?

**Step 3: Start with Postgres unless you have a reason not to**

Postgres is a remarkable default:
- ACID, strong types, rich SQL
- JSONB for semi-structured data
- Full-text search (tsvector)
- Geospatial (PostGIS)
- Time-series (TimescaleDB)
- Pub/sub (LISTEN/NOTIFY)
- Logical replication, CDC (Debezium)
- Extensions: pgvector, pg_trgm, Citus, pg_cron

'Use Postgres for everything' is a valid starting architecture for 90% of apps up to millions of users. Add specialized stores as specific pain demands.

**Step 4: Reach for NoSQL when specific patterns justify it**

- **DynamoDB / Redis KV**: access is purely by key, scale needs horizontal elasticity, or cache/session layer
- **MongoDB**: document shapes vary wildly by record, rapid iteration, no joins needed
- **Cassandra / ScyllaDB**: write throughput exceeds what vertical Postgres can handle (> 100k writes/sec sustained), time-series at massive scale
- **Neo4j**: queries are fundamentally graph traversals (social network followers, fraud rings)

**Step 5: Reach for NewSQL when you need both scale and SQL**

- Global multi-region ACID (CockroachDB, Spanner)
- Outgrew single-node Postgres; want SQL, not NoSQL rewrite
- Accept cross-region commit latency (50–200ms)

**Step 6: Add specialized stores as needed**

- **Elasticsearch**: search and log aggregation (not primary DB)
- **Snowflake/BigQuery**: analytics; separate from OLTP
- **Redis**: cache; don't treat as source of truth
- **S3**: blobs, files, images
- **Vector DB**: RAG / semantic search

**Common scenarios mapped to databases:**

- **E-commerce**: Postgres + Redis cache + Elasticsearch search + S3 images + Snowflake analytics
- **Social network**: Postgres or Cassandra for timeline (depending on scale) + Redis for fanout + Neo4j for relationships + Elasticsearch for search
- **IoT telemetry**: Kafka → TimescaleDB or InfluxDB or ClickHouse + Postgres for metadata
- **Gaming leaderboard**: Redis sorted sets + Postgres for user accounts
- **SaaS with global customers**: CockroachDB or Spanner + regional Redis
- **Content management**: Postgres + MongoDB if shapes vary + Elasticsearch + S3
- **AI / RAG**: pgvector or Pinecone + Postgres metadata

sections.title: CAP, PACELC, and Other Hard Truths
sections.content:
**CAP theorem** (Eric Brewer): in a partition, you choose consistency or availability. In practice, most systems aren't dealing with partitions all the time, so CAP isn't the daily trade-off.

**PACELC** (more useful): in Partition, choose Availability vs Consistency (like CAP). **Else** (normal operation), choose Latency vs Consistency. This captures the real trade-off: even without partitions, stronger consistency requires more coordination, which costs latency.

- Postgres single-node: CP (fails writes if DB unreachable)
- Cassandra: AP (returns stale data during partition)
- DynamoDB: tunable (eventual by default, strong consistent reads opt-in)
- Spanner / CockroachDB: CP (fails writes rather than serve inconsistent)

**Write amplification differs.** Cassandra writes sequential (fast). Postgres btree writes may cause random IO. LSM-tree DBs (Cassandra, RocksDB-backed) are write-optimized; B-tree DBs (Postgres, MySQL InnoDB) are balanced.

**DynamoDB single-table design.** Access patterns drive schema; you can't just add ad-hoc queries later. Requires upfront discipline; GSIs for alternate access patterns. For teams familiar with SQL, the mental model shift is real.

**MongoDB myths.** 'Schema-less' doesn't mean schema-free — your application enforces schema; document validation helps. MongoDB 4.0+ supports multi-document transactions but they're slower; design to avoid.

**Postgres at scale.** Vertical scaling goes far (TBs of data, 10K+ writes/sec per node). Read replicas scale reads. Sharding is manual historically; Citus, PgDog, Spock extensions add horizontal scaling. Postgres at 10TB is normal; at 100TB or 1M+ writes/sec, architecture matters more.

**NoSQL doesn't mean 'no schema'.** You have a schema; it's implicit in your code. Tools like JSON Schema, Avro, Protobuf formalize it. Writing MongoDB without validators = data integrity issues eventually.

**Transactions across systems are hard.** 2PC has operational issues. Use outbox pattern + at-least-once + idempotent consumers. Design for eventual consistency across service boundaries.

**Joins at scale.** Relational joins can be painful at big scale. NoSQL 'solves' this by pre-joining (denormalizing) — you pay write-time cost and storage for read-time speed.

**Managed vs self-hosted.**
- **Managed** (RDS, Atlas, DynamoDB, Aurora, Cockroach Cloud): less ops, more cost, less flexibility
- **Self-hosted**: full control, lower cost, real ops burden (backups, upgrades, HA)

For most teams in 2026, managed is the default; go self-hosted only when specific requirement (compliance, cost-at-huge-scale) justifies.

**Aurora vs RDS vs Postgres on EC2.** Aurora is AWS-rewritten Postgres/MySQL: 3× throughput, shared storage, fast failover, 128TB. More expensive than RDS but better at scale. RDS is managed vanilla Postgres/MySQL. Postgres on EC2 is DIY.

**DynamoDB cost surprises.** At high write volumes, DynamoDB can cost 10× a provisioned RDS instance. Carefully model throughput in test before committing.

**The 'don't use NoSQL for relational data' rule.** If your data has relationships and you'll query them, use a relational DB. Don't rebuild joins in application code.

**Polyglot persistence cost.** Each system adds operational surface. 5 DBs = 5 sets of backups, upgrades, on-call, expertise. Consolidate when possible.

**Data pipeline.** OLTP → OLAP via CDC (Debezium) → Kafka → Snowflake / ClickHouse. Separate concerns; each DB does what it's good at.

**Migration is costly.** Picking the wrong DB early and rewriting later costs months. Err on side of flexibility (Postgres) when uncertain.

**Vector DB freshness.** pgvector is 2–3× slower than specialized (Pinecone, Weaviate) but integrates with your existing Postgres. At moderate scale (tens of millions of vectors), pgvector is fine; beyond, specialize.

**The strategic defaults in 2026:**
- **Start with Postgres** (managed) for OLTP
- **Add Redis** for cache and sessions
- **Add Elasticsearch** for search when SQL LIKE/fulltext isn't enough
- **Add Snowflake / BigQuery** when analytics load strains OLTP
- **Add S3** for blobs
- **Add DynamoDB / Cassandra** only when proven need for horizontal scale
- **Add CockroachDB / Spanner** only when multi-region strong consistency is a hard requirement
- **Add pgvector** for RAG; upgrade to Pinecone/Weaviate at scale

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Default to Postgres** unless you have a specific reason not to — ACID, rich SQL, mature ecosystem
- **NoSQL categories serve specific patterns** — KV, document, wide-column, graph — not 'scale'
- **NewSQL** (CockroachDB, Spanner, YugabyteDB) = SQL + horizontal scale + ACID at latency cost
- **OLTP vs OLAP are different workloads** — don't mix (use data warehouse for analytics)
- **CAP doesn't apply daily**; PACELC captures latency vs consistency trade-off normal-time
- **Polyglot persistence is the norm** — Postgres + Redis + ES + S3 + Snowflake is typical stack
- **Access patterns drive schema** in NoSQL (DynamoDB especially) — can't easily add ad-hoc queries
- **Postgres scales further than people think** — 10TB and 10K+ writes/sec per node are routine
- **Managed > self-hosted** for most teams — less ops surface
- **Join-heavy data wants a relational DB** — don't rebuild joins in app code

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The wrong question is 'SQL or NoSQL'. The right question is 'what are my read/write patterns, consistency needs, and scale requirements?'

**The database landscape in 2026**
- Relational: Postgres, MySQL
- Key-Value: Redis, DynamoDB
- Document: MongoDB, Couchbase
- Wide-column: Cassandra, ScyllaDB
- Graph: Neo4j, Neptune
- NewSQL / Distributed SQL: CockroachDB, Spanner, YugabyteDB
- OLAP / Data warehouse: Snowflake, BigQuery, ClickHouse
- Search: Elasticsearch, OpenSearch
- Time-series: InfluxDB, TimescaleDB
- Vector: Pinecone, Weaviate, pgvector

**Start with Postgres unless you have a reason not to**
- ACID, rich SQL, mature tooling
- JSONB for semi-structured data
- Full-text search, geospatial (PostGIS)
- Time-series (TimescaleDB), pub/sub (LISTEN/NOTIFY)
- Vector (pgvector), logical replication, CDC
- 'Postgres for everything' is a valid starting architecture for 90% of apps

**Reach for NoSQL when specific patterns justify it**
- DynamoDB or Redis KV: access purely by key; horizontal scale needed
- MongoDB: document shapes vary wildly; flexible schema
- Cassandra or ScyllaDB: write throughput beyond single-node Postgres (> 100K writes/sec)
- Neo4j: queries are fundamentally graph traversals

**Reach for NewSQL when you need both scale and SQL**
- Global multi-region ACID
- Outgrew single-node Postgres
- Accept cross-region commit latency (50 to 200ms)

**Add specialized stores as needed**
- Elasticsearch for search (not primary DB)
- Snowflake or BigQuery for analytics
- Redis for cache
- S3 for blobs
- Vector DB for RAG or semantic search

**Decision framework**

*Understand your workload*
- OLTP: short reads/writes, high concurrency, consistency matters
- OLAP: long scans, aggregates, eventual freshness OK
- HTAP: both; usually separate OLTP + pipeline to OLAP
- Real-time streaming: append-heavy time-based
- Search: full-text ranking faceting

*Understand your access patterns*
- How do you read? By key, by range, by join, by text, by similarity?
- How do you write? Append-only, updates in place, bulk?
- Read:write ratio?
- Scale in rows, ops/sec, data size?
- Consistency: strong, read-your-writes, eventual?

**CAP vs PACELC**
- CAP: in partition, choose consistency or availability
- In practice, most systems aren't partitioned all the time
- PACELC captures the real trade-off: in partition, availability vs consistency; else latency vs consistency
- Postgres single-node: CP; Cassandra: AP; DynamoDB: tunable; Spanner: CP

**Common scenarios**
- E-commerce: Postgres + Redis + Elasticsearch + S3 + Snowflake
- Social network: Postgres or Cassandra + Redis + Neo4j + Elasticsearch
- IoT telemetry: Kafka to TimescaleDB or ClickHouse + Postgres metadata
- Gaming leaderboard: Redis sorted sets + Postgres
- Global SaaS: CockroachDB or Spanner + regional Redis
- AI / RAG: pgvector or Pinecone + Postgres metadata

**Common mistakes**
- Defaulting to NoSQL for 'scale' without needing it
- Thinking Postgres doesn't scale (10TB and 10K+ writes/sec routine)
- Picking MongoDB for relational data; rebuilding joins in app code
- Mixing OLTP and OLAP on same DB; analytics queries kill transactional performance
- Under-modeling DynamoDB access patterns; can't add ad-hoc queries later

**Managed vs self-hosted**
- Managed (RDS, Aurora, Atlas, DynamoDB, Cockroach Cloud): less ops, more cost
- Self-hosted: full control, lower cost, real ops burden
- For most teams in 2026, managed is the default

**Aurora vs RDS vs Postgres on EC2**
- Aurora: AWS-rewritten Postgres/MySQL; 3x throughput, shared storage, 128TB
- RDS: managed vanilla Postgres/MySQL
- Postgres on EC2: DIY

**The strategic defaults in 2026**
- Start with Postgres (managed) for OLTP
- Add Redis for cache and sessions
- Add Elasticsearch for search when SQL LIKE isn't enough
- Add Snowflake or BigQuery when analytics strain OLTP
- Add S3 for blobs
- Add DynamoDB or Cassandra only when proven need for horizontal scale
- Add CockroachDB or Spanner only when multi-region strong consistency is hard requirement
- Add pgvector for RAG; upgrade to specialized at scale

**Polyglot persistence cost**
- Each system adds operational surface
- 5 DBs equals 5 sets of backups, upgrades, on-call, expertise
- Consolidate when possible

**The strategic answer**
- Postgres is the default; it's remarkable in 2026
- Reach for specialized stores only when specific patterns justify
- Polyglot persistence is normal but has cost
- Access patterns drive schema in NoSQL, not the other way around
- Managed services are default for most teams
- Don't rebuild joins in application code; use a relational DB
- Migration is costly; err on side of flexibility when uncertain
